How to read the numbers

cells.text: Words multiplied by the agreed rate per word
Check against the quote before delivery
Under 2 with the job still In translation means call the linguist today
Words in jobs marked Delivered for the client
Use for volume discounts and annual reviews
Highest quality-check score on the job
Under 90 means a conversation with the linguist

text.text: Jobs by margin
A good quote is fast, clear and correct. A good assignment puts the right specialist on the job with enough days to do it well.
Quote within four working hours
Get the files, the language pair, the purpose (publish, file with a court, internal use) and the deadline.
Run the analysis and enter the counts on a new job with status
Quoted
Choose the
Service
. Certified translations and transcreation are priced differently from translation and edit.
Send the price, the delivery date and what is included (review, formatting, certification).
What to ask before quoting
Who is the reader, and where will it appear?
Is there a glossary, style guide or earlier translation to follow?
Are the files editable? Scanned PDFs need extra time to prepare.
Does the translation need a certificate or a sworn translator?
Choosing the linguist

cells.text: A legal translator for a contract, a medical one for a leaflet
Words per day against the deadline
A 10,000-word job at 2,500 a day needs four working days plus review
Required before any file is shared

text.text: Assign
Link the linguist and the project manager; set the status to
In translation
Send the files, the glossary terms for that client, the style guide and the due date with a time zone.
Set an internal due date one working day before the client's, so review has time.
Margin check
If
Gross margin
is under 35 percent, look again: a different linguist, a longer deadline, or a higher rate for a rush.
Example

Kestrel's service manual is 18,500 words, with 9,300 matched or repeated. Matteo, a technical English to German specialist, has it at his usual rate and is due nine days from now, with review booked for the last two.
Clients notice inconsistent terms more than anything else. A shared, approved glossary per client makes every linguist sound like one writer.
What goes in the glossary
Product names, part names and features
Legal defined terms ("the Licensee", "the Effective Date")
Medical and regulatory terms that must match approved documents
Interface words such as button labels
Terms the client has said they dislike, with the preferred choice
Approval
A linguist proposes a term with a note on context. It goes in unapproved.
The project manager sends unapproved terms to the client's reviewer in one batch, not one at a time.
Once the client confirms, tick
Approved
. Only approved terms are binding.
Working with linguists
Send the client's approved terms with every job.
Ask linguists to flag new terms rather than invent a translation silently.
After delivery, add any new agreed term the same week.
Keeping it clean

cells.text: Keep the approved one; note the other as not to be used
Add a short note: where it appears, what it means
Keep them, marked as retired, so older documents still make sense

text.text: Style guides
Tick
Style guide on file

on the client when you have one. A style guide covers tone, formal or informal address, numbers and dates, and brand rules. If a client has none, write a one-page version after the first job and ask them to confirm it.
Review twice a year
Unapproved terms older than 60 days chased or removed
Terms used in recent jobs checked for consistency
New linguists given the glossary and style guide
Example
Kestrel's "torque limit" is still waiting on their engineering review. Until it is approved, Matteo uses the term from the last delivered manual and flags it in his delivery note.
Every job gets a second pair of eyes before it reaches the client. A simple error count keeps reviews fair and shows where to help a linguist improve.
How the review works
Schedule the review when the job moves to
In review
The reviewer compares the translation with the source, checking meaning, terms, numbers, names, formatting and style.
Each problem is counted by severity and returned to the linguist to fix.
The reviewer gives a score out of 100 and a result.
Severity, in plain words

cells.text: Wrong dosage, wrong amount, a clause that changes meaning
Wrong term from the glossary, a missing sentence, a mistranslation that confuses
Punctuation, a slightly awkward phrase, a spacing slip

text.text: Results
Pass
: no critical and no major errors.
Pass after fixes
: major errors found and corrected before delivery.
Fail
: any critical error, or many majors. The job goes back, and the project manager decides whether a second linguist should help.
Feedback to linguists
Send the marked file and a short note: what was good and what to watch. Patterns matter more than single slips. Three major errors of the same kind across jobs is a conversation, not a scolding.
Reviewer checklist
Glossary terms used everywhere they apply
Numbers, dates, units and names checked against the source
Nothing left untranslated or duplicated
Formatting matches the source file
Spelling and grammar check run in the target language
Reviewing the reviewers

Once a quarter, the project manager spot-checks a few reviewed jobs. A reviewer who never finds anything, or who marks preferences as errors, needs a word. Rotate reviewers on big accounts so one person's habits do not become the client's style by accident.
Example
The distribution agreement passed after fixes: one major error, a defined term used inconsistently, was corrected before delivery, and the term was added to the glossary.
Delivery is where the client sees the work. A tidy delivery and a short follow-up turn one job into a steady account.
Before you deliver
Review result is Pass or Pass after fixes
Files open correctly in the client's format
File names follow the client's convention, with the language code
Certificate attached when the service is certified translation
Any open questions listed in the delivery note
Deliver
Send the files with a short note: what is included, any terms the client should confirm, and the PO number.
Set the job to
Delivered
with the date.
Update the translation memory and the glossary the same day.
Invoicing
Invoice from the job price; quote the client's PO number.
Rush and weekend work is charged as agreed in the quote, never added afterwards.
Pay linguists on the agreed schedule. Paying on time keeps your best people.
Follow-up
One week after delivery, ask if the reviewers had any changes.
Client changes that are preferences, not errors, go into the glossary or style guide so they do not repeat.
Errors found by the client get logged as a review note and discussed with the linguist.
Measuring the month

cells.text: Jobs, filtered by delivered after due
Jobs by margin on the dashboard

text.text: When a client is unhappy

Listen first, then look at the file together. Separate real errors from taste. Fix errors at no charge and quickly; record preferences so they never come up again. A calm, fast answer to a complaint keeps more clients than a perfect first delivery.
Example
The hotel partner brochure was delivered on time with two tone corrections. A week later the client asked for a warmer phrase on the cover, which is now a note in their style guide.

The translation tool holds the files and the translation memory. This workspace holds the business around them: who asked for what, who is translating it, when it is due, what it costs and what it earns.

Service, pair, source files, word counts from the analysis, weighted words, price, linguist cost, margin, dates, project manager
Approved and pending terms per client and pair
Score, errors by severity and the result

text.text: How a job is priced
Run the file analysis in your translation tool.
Enter
Words
(the total),
Partial matches
and
Repetitions and full matches
Weighted words
takes 40 percent off partial matches and 75 percent off repetitions and full matches. Change the discounts in the formula to match your price list.
Job price
is weighted words times the agreed rate;
Linguist cost
uses the linguist's rate on the same words;
Gross margin
is what is left.
Your first week
Add current clients and note who has a style guide.
Add linguists with pair, specialty, rate and certification. Tick the confidentiality agreement only once it is signed.
Enter open jobs with their analysis, rates and due dates.
Move the most used terms for your biggest clients into the glossary.
The daily rhythm
Morning:
Jobs, Overdue and Due this week. Anything In review due within a day gets the reviewer's time first.
Midday:
check new requests; quote within four working hours.
End of day:
linguists' progress noted; status moved forward honestly.
Buttons
Job buttons move a job to the next stage or schedule a review; review buttons mark a review checked.
Example

The clinical study report summary is In review and due tomorrow. Its 11,200 words include 4,500 matched or repeated words, so the client pays for about 8,700 weighted words, and the margin is 45 percent.
